course.title: Python Programming
course.tagline: Learn Python from zero and write real programs that automate work, handle data and solve problems.

days.title: Install Python and Write Your First Program
days.goal: Install Python on your computer and run your very first line of code.
steps: Go to python.org, download Python for your computer, and install it. Tick the box that says Add Python to PATH.
Open your terminal or command prompt and type python --version to check it installed.
Open VS Code, create a folder called python-journey, and make a file called hello.py.
Type print('Hello, world!') in the file, save it, and run it with python hello.py.
days.task: Write a program that prints your name, your age and one thing you want to build.
days.challenge: Print a simple picture made of text characters, like a smiley face or a small house.

quiz.q: What does print('Hello') do in Python?
options: It saves the word Hello to a file
It shows Hello on the screen
quiz.explain: print shows text on the screen. It is the simplest way to see what your program is doing.

quiz.q: Why do you tick 'Add Python to PATH' during install?
options: It lets you run python from any folder in the terminal
quiz.explain: Adding Python to PATH lets your computer find the python command from any folder.

quiz.q: What file ending do Python files use?
quiz.explain: Python files end in .py.

days.title: Print, Input and Comments
days.goal: Show text on screen, ask the user questions, and leave notes in your code.
steps: Use print() to show three lines of text, one per line.
Use input() to ask the user their name, then print a greeting with their name.
Add a comment with # to explain what one line of your code does.
Run the program twice with different names and watch the greeting change.
days.task: Build a small program that asks for a name and a favourite food, then prints a sentence using both.
days.challenge: Ask the user for two words and print them joined into one funny sentence.

options: It waits for the user to type something and gives it back as text
quiz.explain: input() pauses the program, waits for typing, and returns what was typed as text.

quiz.q: What is a comment in Python?
options: A line that starts with # and is ignored by Python
A line that prints an error
A line that saves a file
quiz.explain: Comments start with # and are notes for humans. Python ignores them when it runs.

quiz.q: What type of data does input() always give you?
quiz.explain: input() always returns text, even if the user types digits. You must convert it to a number to do maths.

days.title: Variables and Data Types
days.goal: Store values in variables and know the difference between text, numbers and true/false values.
steps: Create a variable called name and store your name in it, then print it.
Create age as a number and is_student as True or False, then print all three.
Use type() to check the type of each variable and print the results.
Change the value of a variable and print it again to see the new value.
days.task: Make a small profile program with variables for name, age, city and a hobby, then print them in neat sentences.
days.challenge: Swap the values of two variables using a third temporary variable.

options: A named box that stores a value
quiz.explain: A variable is a name that stores a value you can use and change later.

quiz.q: Which of these is a valid variable name?
quiz.explain: Variable names can use letters, numbers and underscores, but cannot start with a number or contain spaces or dashes.

quiz.q: What is the type of the value True?
quiz.explain: True and False are booleans, used for yes/no and on/off values.

days.title: Numbers and Maths
days.goal: Do maths in Python: add, subtract, multiply, divide and work with remainders.
steps: Try print(10 + 5), print(10 - 5), print(10 * 5) and print(10 / 5) in the terminal.
Use // for whole-number division and % to get the remainder of a division.
Use ** to raise a number to a power, like 2 ** 3.
Ask the user for two numbers, turn them into numbers with int(), and print their sum.
days.task: Build a simple calculator that asks for two numbers and prints the sum, difference, product and division.
days.challenge: Work out how many minutes are in a week using only Python maths, then print the answer.

quiz.explain: % gives the remainder. 10 divided by 3 leaves 1.

options: It turns the text '7' into the number 7
quiz.explain: int() turns text that looks like a whole number into a real number you can calculate with.
** means to the power of. 2 to the power of 3 is 2 x 2 x 2 = 8.

days.title: Strings and Text
days.goal: Work with text: join strings, repeat them, slice them and use f-strings.
steps: Join two strings with + and print the result.
Use an f-string like f'My name is {name}' to put a variable inside text.
Use len() to count the letters in a word and print the count.
Slice a string with [0:3] to get the first three letters and print them.
days.task: Build a program that asks for a first name and last name, then prints the full name in capital letters and its length.
days.challenge: Ask for a sentence and print it backwards using slicing [::-1].

options: A string with a file inside it
A string that lets you put variables inside curly braces {}
A string that is always false
A string that cannot be printed
quiz.explain: An f-string starts with f and lets you drop variables straight into text with {name}.
len() counts characters. 'hello' has 5 letters.
Multiplying a string repeats it. 'ha' times 3 is 'hahaha'.

days.title: Lists
days.goal: Store many items in one list, add and remove items, and read items by position.

video.title: Python Full Course | Python Tutorial for Beginners | Part 1

steps: Make a list of five favourite foods and print the whole list.
Print the first item with foods[0] and the last item with foods[-1].
Add a new food with append() and remove one with remove(), then print the list again.
Use len() to count how many items are in the list.
days.task: Make a shopping list program that starts with three items, adds two more, removes one, and prints the final list.
days.challenge: Make a list of numbers and print the biggest with max(), the smallest with min() and the total with sum().

quiz.q: What position does the first item in a list have?
quiz.explain: Lists start counting at 0. The first item is at index 0.

options: It adds an item to the end of a list
quiz.explain: append() adds one new item to the end of a list.
A negative index counts from the end. -1 is the last item.

days.title: Project 1: Number Guessing Game
days.goal: Combine everything from week 1 into a working game.
steps: Import the random module and use random.randint(1, 20) to pick a secret number.
Ask the player to guess and tell them if the guess is too high or too low.
Keep asking until they guess right, and count how many tries it took.
Print a win message with the number of tries when they get it right.
days.task: Finish the guessing game and play it three times to check it works.
days.challenge: Add a limit of 5 guesses. If the player runs out, reveal the secret number.

options: It picks a random whole number between 1 and 20
quiz.explain: randint(a, b) returns a random whole number from a to b, including both ends.

quiz.q: Which loop is best for asking until the player guesses right?
quiz.explain: A while loop repeats until a condition changes, which fits 'keep asking until correct'.

quiz.q: Why do we convert the guess with int()?
options: Because input() gives text and we need a number to compare
To save it to a file
quiz.explain: input() returns text. int() turns it into a number so you can compare it with the secret number.

project.title: Number Guessing Game
project.brief: Build a complete guessing game: the computer picks a secret number from 1 to 20, the player guesses, and the game gives hints until the player wins.
checks: The computer picks a random number from 1 to 20.
The player can type a guess and the game reads it.
The game says 'too high' or 'too low' after each wrong guess.
The game counts the number of tries.
The game prints a win message when the guess is right.
The game handles a guess that is not a number without crashing.

days.title: If, Else and Comparisons
days.goal: Make decisions in code with if, elif and else.

video.title: Python Full Course for Beginners to Advanced | 12 Hours

steps: Write an if statement that prints 'Adult' when age is 18 or more.
Add an elif for age 13 to 17 that prints 'Teenager', and an else that prints 'Child'.
Try the comparison operators ==, !=, > and < in small tests.
Combine two checks with and and or, for example age >= 18 and has_id.
days.task: Build a program that asks for a test score and prints A, B, C or F based on the score.
days.challenge: Ask for a password. Print 'Welcome' only if it matches, otherwise print 'Wrong password'.

quiz.explain: == compares two values for equality. A single = assigns a value.

quiz.q: When does the else block run?
options: Only when the if (and elif) checks are all false
quiz.explain: else runs only when every check above it was false.

quiz.q: What does 'and' do in a condition?
options: It joins two conditions and both must be true
quiz.explain: and means both sides must be true for the whole condition to be true.

days.title: Loops: for
days.goal: Repeat work with for loops over lists and number ranges.

video.title: Python Full Course for Beginners | Complete Python & PyTest Tutorial

steps: Use for name in names: to print every name in a list.
Use range(5) to print the numbers 0 to 4.
Use range(1, 11) to print the numbers 1 to 10.
Add up all the numbers in a list with a for loop and print the total.
days.task: Print the 5 times table from 5 x 1 to 5 x 12 using a for loop.
days.challenge: Loop through a list of words and print only the words longer than 4 letters.

quiz.explain: range(3) gives 0, 1, 2. It stops before 3.

quiz.q: What does a for loop do?
options: It runs code once for each item in a sequence
It asks the user a question
quiz.explain: A for loop repeats its block once for each item in a list, string or range.

quiz.q: What does break do inside a loop?
quiz.explain: break exits the loop straight away, even if items remain.

days.title: Loops: while
days.goal: Repeat work with while loops and stop them safely.

video.title: Learn Object Oriented Programming With Python

steps: Write a while loop that counts from 1 to 5 and prints each number.
Make a loop that keeps asking for a password until the right one is typed.
Use a counter variable and increase it inside the loop so the loop can end.
Add a break that stops the loop when the user types 'quit'.
days.task: Build a small menu that keeps showing options until the user picks 'Exit'.
days.challenge: Use a while loop to keep doubling a number until it passes 1000, then print how many steps it took.

quiz.q: When does a while loop stop?
quiz.explain: A while loop keeps going while its condition is true and stops when it becomes false.

options: A loop that runs forever because its condition never becomes false
A loop that prints forever by choice
A loop that only runs once
quiz.explain: An infinite loop never ends because nothing inside it changes the condition to false.

quiz.q: What does continue do in a loop?
options: It skips the rest of this round and starts the next one
quiz.explain: continue jumps straight to the next round of the loop, skipping the code below it.

days.title: Functions
days.goal: Write your own functions to reuse code and keep programs tidy.
steps: Define a function greet(name) that prints a greeting, then call it with your name.
Write a function add(a, b) that returns the sum, and print add(3, 4).
Give a function a default value, like greet(name='friend'), and call it with no argument.
Write a function that takes a list of numbers and returns the average.
days.task: Write three functions: one to convert Celsius to Fahrenheit, one for the reverse, and a small menu that uses them.
days.challenge: Write a function that takes a sentence and returns how many words it has.

quiz.explain: def starts the definition of a function, followed by its name and brackets.

options: It sends a value back to the place that called the function
quiz.explain: return hands a value back to the caller so it can be stored or printed.

options: To reuse code, avoid repeating yourself and keep programs tidy
quiz.explain: Functions let you write a piece of logic once and use it many times.

days.title: Dictionaries
days.goal: Store data as key-value pairs and look things up by name.
steps: Make a dictionary for a person with keys name, age and city, then print it.
Print one value with person['name'].
Add a new key and change an existing value, then print the dictionary again.
Loop through the dictionary and print each key and value.
days.task: Build a small phone book: store five names with phone numbers, then look up a number by name.
days.challenge: Count how many times each word appears in a sentence using a dictionary.

quiz.q: What is a dictionary in Python?
quiz.explain: A dictionary stores pairs: each key has a value, like a real dictionary has words with meanings.

quiz.q: How do you get the value for the key 'age'?
quiz.explain: Square brackets with the key, person['age'], give you the value.

options: It returns None instead of an error when the key is missing
quiz.explain: .get() returns None (or a default you choose) when the key is missing, instead of crashing.

days.title: Working with Files
days.goal: Read from and write to text files on your computer.
steps: Create a file called notes.txt and write three lines into it with open() and write().
Read the file back with read() and print what is inside.
Use a with open(...) block so the file closes itself.
Add a new line to the end of the file without deleting what is there.
days.task: Build a simple diary program: each entry you type is saved to diary.txt with today's date.
days.challenge: Read a file and count how many lines and words it has.

options: It opens the file for writing and erases what was there
quiz.explain: 'w' mode opens a file for writing and clears its old content. Use 'a' to add without erasing.

options: It closes the file for you automatically, even if an error happens
quiz.explain: with makes sure the file is closed properly when the block ends.

options: The whole file content as one string
quiz.explain: read() returns the entire file content as a single string.

days.title: Project 2: To-Do List App
days.goal: Build a console app that saves tasks to a file.

video.title: Build a Pomodoro Timer App in Python

steps: Make a list to hold tasks and a menu with Add, Show, Done and Quit.
Save the tasks to tasks.txt every time one is added or removed.
Load the tasks from the file when the program starts.
Let the user mark a task as done by its number.
days.task: Finish the to-do app and test it: add three tasks, close the program, open it again and check they are still there.
days.challenge: Add due dates to tasks and show them in the list.

quiz.q: Why save tasks to a file?
options: So the tasks are still there the next time you open the program
quiz.explain: Data in memory disappears when the program closes. A file keeps it between runs.

quiz.q: Which mode adds to a file without erasing it?
quiz.explain: 'a' (append) adds new content to the end of a file without deleting what is there.

quiz.q: What should the program do at startup?
options: Load saved tasks from the file if it exists
quiz.explain: At startup it should read the saved file so the user sees their old tasks.

project.title: To-Do List App
project.brief: Build a console to-do list app with a menu: add tasks, show tasks, mark tasks done and quit. Tasks must be saved to a file so they survive closing the program.
checks: A menu shows Add, Show, Done and Quit options.
Adding a task stores it in a list.
Showing tasks lists them with numbers.
Marking a task done removes it from the list.
Tasks are saved to a file and loaded when the program starts.
The program handles an empty list and bad menu choices kindly.

days.title: Modules and pip
days.goal: Use other people's code with import and install packages with pip.
steps: Import the math module and use math.sqrt(16) and math.pi.
Import random and use random.choice() to pick a random item from a list.
Use pip install requests in the terminal to install a package.
Import requests and check its version.
days.task: Write a program that uses the datetime module to print today's date and the day of the week.
days.challenge: Use the random module to shuffle a list of quiz questions and ask them in a random order.

options: A file of Python code you can import and reuse
quiz.explain: A module is a Python file with useful functions and values you can import into your own code.

options: It installs Python packages from the internet
quiz.explain: pip is Python's package installer. pip install requests downloads and installs the requests package.

quiz.q: What does import math let you do?
options: It gives you extra maths functions like sqrt and pi
quiz.explain: Importing math gives you ready-made maths tools like square root, pi and rounding.

days.title: Error Handling
days.goal: Stop crashes with try and except, and handle bad input kindly.
steps: Wrap a division in try/except and print a friendly message when dividing by zero.
Ask the user for a number inside a try block and catch the error if they type letters.
Use except ValueError for bad numbers and except ZeroDivisionError for zero division.
Add a finally block that prints 'Done' no matter what happens.
days.task: Make your calculator catch bad input and division by zero, and keep asking until it gets valid numbers.
days.challenge: Try opening a file that does not exist and catch the FileNotFoundError with a helpful message.

options: It tries code and runs a backup plan if an error happens
It deletes errors from the file
quiz.explain: try runs code that might fail. If it fails, except runs instead of crashing the program.

quiz.q: What error happens when you turn 'abc' into a number with int()?
quiz.explain: int('abc') raises a ValueError because the text cannot be turned into a number.

options: It runs only when there is no error
It runs whether or not an error happened
quiz.explain: finally runs at the end no matter what, which is handy for closing files or cleaning up.

days.title: Classes and Objects 1
days.goal: Understand objects: a class is a blueprint and an object is a thing built from it.
steps: Define a class Dog with an __init__ that stores name and age.
Make two Dog objects with different names and print their names.
Add a method bark() that prints the dog's name plus 'says woof!'.
Call bark() on both dogs and see the different results.
days.task: Make a Book class with title, author and pages, plus a method that prints a short summary.
days.challenge: Make a class for a bank account with a balance, and methods to deposit and withdraw money.

quiz.explain: A class is a blueprint. It describes what data and actions its objects will have.

options: A method that runs when you create a new object
A method that deletes an object
quiz.explain: __init__ is the setup method. It runs automatically when you create an object and stores its starting values.

quiz.q: What does self mean inside a method?
options: The object itself, so the method can reach its own data
quiz.explain: self refers to the object the method was called on, so it can read and change that object's data.

days.title: Classes and Objects 2
days.goal: Use methods, attributes and string representations to make classes useful.
steps: Add a __str__ method to your Book class so printing a book shows a nice sentence.
Add a method is_long() that returns True when a book has more than 300 pages.
Add a class attribute that counts how many objects have been made.
Make a method that updates an attribute, like change_price().
days.task: Build a Student class with name, scores and a method that returns the average score.
days.challenge: Add a method to your bank account that refuses a withdrawal bigger than the balance.

options: It decides what shows when you print the object
It saves the object to a file
quiz.explain: __str__ returns the text Python shows when you print an object.

options: A function defined inside a class that works on objects
quiz.explain: A method is a function inside a class. It usually works with the object's data through self.

options: A piece of data stored on an object, like name or age
quiz.explain: Attributes are the data an object holds, such as a dog's name or a book's page count.

days.title: Inheritance
days.goal: Reuse code by making a child class that builds on a parent class.
steps: Make a parent class Animal with a speak() method.
Make a child class Cat that inherits from Animal and changes speak() to meow.
Use super() to reuse the parent's __init__ in the child.
Make a Dog child class and call speak() on both.
days.task: Build a Vehicle parent class and Car and Bike child classes with their own extra methods.
days.challenge: Add a method to the parent that the children inherit unchanged, and test it on both.

options: A child class getting the parent class's methods and data
quiz.explain: Inheritance lets a child class reuse and extend a parent class instead of rewriting the same code.

options: It calls the parent class's method from the child
quiz.explain: super() lets a child class call the parent's method, often to reuse its setup code.

quiz.q: What happens when a child defines the same method as the parent?
quiz.explain: The child's method overrides the parent's. The child version runs for child objects.

days.title: Automation: Files and Folders
days.goal: Automate boring computer jobs with Python and the os module.
steps: Use os.listdir() to list the files in a folder.
Use os to make a new folder if it does not exist.
Write a script that moves all .jpg files into a folder called Images.
Rename files in a loop, adding a number to each name.
days.task: Build a downloads cleaner: sort files in a folder into Images, Documents and Others folders.
days.challenge: Write a script that finds files bigger than 10 MB in a folder and lists them.

quiz.q: What does the os module help with?
options: Working with files, folders and the operating system
quiz.explain: os gives you tools to list folders, make folders, move files and more.

options: A list of file and folder names in that folder
quiz.explain: listdir returns the names of everything inside a folder.

options: It is slower than by hand
It saves time and avoids mistakes when there are many files
quiz.explain: A script can sort hundreds of files in a second with no mistakes.

days.title: Project 3: Pomodoro Timer
days.goal: Build a focus timer that counts down and reminds you to take breaks.
steps: Ask the user how many minutes to focus for.
Use the time module and sleep(1) to count down second by second.
Print the remaining time each second in minutes and seconds.
When time is up, print a message and play a sound or print a bell character.
days.task: Finish the Pomodoro timer with 25 minutes of focus, a 5 minute break, and four rounds.
days.challenge: Add a log file that records each finished focus session with the date and time.

options: It pauses the program for one second
quiz.explain: sleep(1) pauses your program for one second, which is how you build a countdown.

options: Because the computer counts in seconds and you can format them into minutes
Because time only exists in seconds
Because sleep() only works with seconds
quiz.explain: sleep() works in seconds, so you count seconds and show them as minutes and seconds.

quiz.q: What does the datetime module give you?
quiz.explain: datetime lets you read the current date and time and do maths with dates.

project.title: Pomodoro Focus Timer
project.brief: Build a Pomodoro timer: 25 minutes of focus, then a 5 minute break, for four rounds. Show the countdown live and log each finished session to a file.
checks: The timer counts down from the chosen minutes in seconds.
The remaining time shows as minutes and seconds.
A message appears when focus time ends and when break time ends.
The timer runs four focus rounds with breaks between them.
Each finished session is written to a log file with the date.
The user can set the focus length at the start.

days.title: Build a Calculator App
days.goal: Put functions, loops and error handling together in one useful app.

video.title: Python Full Course | Python Tutorial for Beginners | Part 1

steps: Write add, subtract, multiply and divide functions.
Show a menu and keep it running in a while loop until the user quits.
Catch bad input with try/except so the app never crashes.
Add a history list that shows the last five calculations.
days.task: Finish the calculator and test every operation, including dividing by zero.
days.challenge: Add a power and square root option to the menu.

quiz.q: Why keep the menu in a while loop?
options: So the user can do many calculations without restarting
quiz.explain: A while loop keeps the menu showing until the user chooses to quit.

options: So each operation is easy to test, fix and reuse
quiz.explain: One function per operation keeps the code tidy and each piece easy to check.

quiz.q: What should dividing by zero do in your app?
options: Show a friendly message and let the user try again
quiz.explain: A good app catches the error and explains it, instead of crashing.

days.title: Reading Data from the Web
days.goal: Fetch a web page with requests and read what comes back.
steps: Install requests with pip install requests.
Use requests.get() to fetch a simple web page and print the status code.
Print the first 200 characters of the page text.
Check that a 200 status code means the page loaded fine.
days.task: Fetch a public API that returns a joke or a quote and print the joke or quote.
days.challenge: Fetch three different pages and print each one's status code.

options: A way for programs to ask another service for data
quiz.explain: An API is a set of rules that lets your program request data from another service, like weather or jokes.

options: Everything worked, the page loaded fine
quiz.explain: 200 means OK. The request worked and the server sent back what you asked for.

options: A response object with the status code and content
quiz.explain: get() returns a response object. You can read .status_code and .text from it.

days.title: Working with APIs and JSON
days.goal: Read JSON data from an API and use it in your program.

video.title: Python Full Course for Beginners to Advanced | 12 Hours

steps: Fetch a JSON API and use .json() to turn the reply into Python data.
Print one value from the data, like the title of a post.
Loop through a list in the JSON and print each item.
Handle the case where the request fails with a friendly message.
days.task: Build a small program that fetches the current weather for a city and prints the temperature and description.
days.challenge: Fetch a list of users from a public API and print only their names and emails.

options: A text format for sending data, with keys and values
quiz.explain: JSON is a plain-text format for data, using curly braces and key-value pairs, like Python dictionaries.

options: It turns JSON text into Python dictionaries and lists
quiz.explain: .json() parses the JSON text into Python data you can work with.

quiz.q: Why check the status code before reading JSON?
options: Because a failed request may not contain valid JSON
quiz.explain: If the request failed, the reply may be an error page, not JSON, and parsing it would crash.

days.title: Data with CSV Files
days.goal: Read and write spreadsheet-style CSV files with Python.

video.title: Python Full Course for Beginners | Complete Python & PyTest Tutorial

steps: Use the csv module to read a CSV file and print each row.
Count how many rows the file has.
Write a new CSV file with a header row and three rows of data.
Use a dictionary to store one row and write it with DictWriter.
days.task: Make an expense tracker: save expenses to expenses.csv and print the total spent.
days.challenge: Read a CSV of scores and print the highest, lowest and average score.

options: A text file where values are separated by commas, like a simple spreadsheet
quiz.explain: CSV stands for comma-separated values. Each line is a row and commas split the columns.

options: It reads a CSV and gives each row as a dictionary using the header as keys
quiz.explain: DictReader turns each row into a dictionary, so you can read row['name'] instead of counting columns.

quiz.q: Why use the csv module instead of splitting text by hand?
options: It handles commas inside quotes and new lines correctly
quiz.explain: Real CSV data can have commas inside values. The csv module handles those cases safely.

days.title: Turtle Graphics Game
days.goal: Draw and make a small game with the turtle module.

video.title: Learn Object Oriented Programming With Python

steps: Import turtle, make a turtle, and draw a square with a loop.
Change the pen colour and draw a circle.
Use the arrow keys to move the turtle with onkey().
Make the turtle move forward on its own in a loop.
days.task: Draw a simple house with turtle: a square, a triangle roof and a door.
days.challenge: Make a turtle race: three turtles race to the right edge with random steps.

options: A drawing tool that moves a turtle around the screen to draw shapes
quiz.explain: turtle is a simple drawing tool. You tell a turtle to move and turn, and it draws as it goes.

options: It moves the turtle 100 steps in the direction it faces
quiz.explain: forward(100) moves the turtle 100 pixels forward, drawing a line if the pen is down.

options: It runs a function when you press a key
quiz.explain: onkey() links a keyboard key to a function, so pressing the key runs your code.

days.title: Build a Quiz Game
days.goal: Build a quiz that asks questions, keeps score and shows a result.
steps: Store questions as a list of dictionaries with question, options and answer.
Ask each question, read the answer and check if it is right.
Add one point for each right answer and show the score at the end.
Print a different message for a perfect score, a good score and a low score.
days.task: Finish the quiz with at least 5 questions about Python and test it on a friend.
days.challenge: Shuffle the questions each time the quiz runs so the order changes.

quiz.q: Why store questions in a list of dictionaries?
options: So each question keeps its text, options and answer together in one tidy place
quiz.explain: A dictionary keeps each question's text, options and correct answer together, and a list holds them all in order.

options: It mixes a list into a random order
quiz.explain: shuffle() rearranges a list into a random order in place.

quiz.q: How do you keep score in a quiz?
options: With a number variable that grows by 1 for each right answer

quiz.q: What does a traceback tell you?
options: Which line failed and what kind of error happened
quiz.explain: A traceback shows the error type and the exact line where it happened, which is your best clue.

Add comments that explain the tricky parts.

options: A file that explains what a project does and how to use it

quiz.q: Why clean up code before sharing it?

quiz.q: What makes a good project demo?
options: A clear explanation of the problem, the solution and a live run

quiz.q: What should your capstone plan include?
options: The problem, the features, the tools used and how you will show it

capstone.title: Build and Share a Python Automation Tool
capstone.brief: Build a Python tool that automates a real daily job: a downloads folder cleaner, an expense tracker, or a daily report maker. It must read or write files, handle errors kindly, and be shared on GitHub with a README and a short demo.
checks: The tool solves one real daily problem and you can explain the problem in one sentence.
It reads from or writes to files on the computer.
It uses at least one function you wrote and one loop.
It handles bad input and missing files with try/except instead of crashing.
It has a README that explains what it does and how to run it.
The code is on GitHub in a public repository.
You can show a live demo and explain how it works in simple words.
deliverables: A working Python automation tool (the .py file).
A README.md explaining the problem, the features and how to run it.
A public GitHub repository link with the code.
A short demo video or screenshots showing the tool running.
A one-page write-up of what you learned in 30 days.
